lessons.title: Initial Incision and Bleeding Procedures
lessons.body: After stunning, the beast must be bled immediately. For a 410 kg beast, you have about 60 seconds to start bleeding after stunning. Use a sharp 6-inch curved boning knife. Stand to the side, not in front. Make a 15 cm incision just below the jaw, from the throat up toward the ear. Cut deep to sever the carotid artery and jugular vein. Blood will spurt; let it drain into a trough. For 410 beasts, you need a bleeding rail or hoist that holds at least 500 kg. Hang the beast by its hind legs using a steel gambrel and chain. The bleed time is 4 to 6 minutes. Collect blood in a clean container if you plan to use it for food; otherwise, direct it to a drain. In Africa, many small abattoirs use a simple A-frame with a block and tackle. Ensure the floor is sloped to a blood pit. Wear gumboots, apron, and gloves. After bleeding, check for signs of consciousness; if the beast blinks or breathes, bleed again. Never leave a beast half-bled. Move to the next step only when bleeding stops. This step is critical for meat quality and safety.

lessons.title: Evisceration Steps for 410 Beasts
lessons.body: Evisceration means removing the internal organs. Start by making a cut from the sternum down to the pelvic bone. Use a sharp knife and keep the blade pointed up to avoid cutting the intestines. For a 410 kg beast, the belly is tight; use a meat saw to split the sternum. Then, with your hand, push the intestines aside and cut the diaphragm. Reach in and pull the esophagus and trachea down. Tie off the rectum with a string to prevent feces spill. Now, pull the intestines out gently. Place them in a clean wheelbarrow or tray. Next, remove the liver, heart, and lungs. For 410 beasts, you need a team of three: one cuts, one holds, one inspects. Work on a rail system at waist height. In Africa, many use a simple pulley hoist. After removing the guts, wash the carcass with clean water. If you accidentally cut the intestines, wash the area with 1% vinegar solution. Keep the offal separate. The whole evisceration should take 12 to 15 minutes per beast. Speed matters to prevent bacterial growth. Always wear chainmail gloves to protect your hands. Dispose of waste in a pit or incinerator. This step is the most risky for contamination, so be careful.

lessons.title: Carcass Splitting and Trimming
lessons.body: After evisceration, split the carcass down the spine. Use a meat saw or a cleaver. For a 410 kg beast, the spine is thick; you need a saw with a 30-inch blade. Start at the pelvic bone and cut up to the neck. Keep the cut straight to avoid damaging the loin. Then, trim off any bruises, blood clots, and dirt. Use a sharp knife to remove the tail, hooves, and head if not already removed. For African conditions, use a clean cloth to wipe the carcass with a 2% salt solution. This helps prevent flies. Trim excess fat to 1 cm thickness. Remove the spinal cord if required by your market. Split the carcass into two halves. Each half should weigh about 205 kg. Hang the halves on rails. Wash with potable water at 10Â°C. Then, move to the cold room within 30 minutes. In many African abattoirs, splitting is done manually with a hand saw. It takes 8 to 10 minutes per beast. Always wear a mesh apron and gloves. Keep your knives sharp; a dull knife tears meat. After splitting, inspect for abscesses or tumors. Cut them out and discard. This step prepares the carcass for chilling.

lessons.title: Organ Inspection and Disposal
lessons.body: After evisceration, inspect all organs for disease. Look at the liver: it should be smooth, dark red, and free of spots. If you see white spots or hard lumps, it may be liver fluke or tuberculosis. Cut into the liver to check for abscesses. The lungs should be pink and spongy; if they are dark or have foam, the beast may have pneumonia. The heart should be firm and clean. The intestines should be free of ulcers or blood. For 410 beasts, you must inspect each organ. In Africa, common diseases include foot-and-mouth and anthrax. If you suspect anthrax, do not open the carcass; call a veterinarian immediately. For disposal, condemn any organ that is abnormal. Put condemned organs in a pit and cover with lime. Or burn them in an incinerator. Never sell diseased organs. Keep a record of what you condemn. Use a clean table for inspection. Wear gloves and wash hands after. For 410 beasts, you need a team of two inspectors. This step protects public health. It also helps you identify sick animals early. Always follow your country's meat inspection laws.

lessons.title: Hygiene Practices During Evisceration
lessons.body: Hygiene during evisceration is critical. You must wash your hands and knives often. Use a 200 ppm chlorine solution to sanitize knives. For 410 beasts, set up a sanitizer bucket at each station. Wear clean gumboots, a waterproof apron, and gloves. Change gloves if they tear. Do not touch your face or phone. Keep the floor clean; wash away blood and manure. Use a high-pressure hose. In Africa, water can be scarce, so use a bucket with a tap. After each beast, rinse the area. The carcass must not touch the floor. Keep it on the rail. If you drop a knife, sanitize it before use. Use separate knives for opening the belly and for cutting meat. Never use the same knife for both. For 410 beasts, you will process many animals; fatigue can lead to mistakes. Take short breaks. Wash your hands with soap and water for 20 seconds. Use a nail brush. After evisceration, clean all surfaces with detergent and then sanitizer. This step prevents E. coli and Salmonella. It also keeps the meat safe for consumers. Remember, clean meat sells better.

lessons.title: Equipment Sanitization After Evisceration
lessons.body: After evisceration, you must clean and sanitize all equipment. This includes knives, saws, hooks, rails, and tables. First, rinse off blood and tissue with warm water. Then, scrub with a brush and detergent. Use a 200 ppm chlorine solution or a commercial sanitizer. For 410 beasts, you will have a lot of equipment. Set up a three-compartment sink: wash, rinse, sanitize. Soak knives for 2 minutes in sanitizer. For saws, disassemble and clean the blade. Hooks and rails should be wiped with a sanitized cloth. In Africa, many use a simple bucket system. After sanitizing, air-dry the equipment. Do not use a dirty cloth to dry. Store knives in a clean rack. Clean the floor with a hose and disinfectant. Remove all solid waste to a covered bin. For 410 beasts, this cleaning takes about 30 minutes. Assign one person to sanitize while others continue. Always wear gloves when handling sanitizer. Keep a log of when you clean. This step prevents cross-contamination between batches. It also extends the life of your tools. A clean abattoir is a profitable abattoir.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Evisceration and Carcass Preparation for 410 Beasts

This practical reference is written for commercial abattoir operators, cold room managers, and agribusiness teams handling a throughput of 410 beasts per processing cycle. Whether you are running cattle, goats, sheep, or a mixed line, evisceration is the single highest-risk stage for both food safety and carcass value. Done right, it protects yield, shelf life, and export eligibility. Done wrong, it destroys organs, contaminates muscle, and can shut down your cold room operation under inspection. This module gives you the operational detail you need to train staff, standardise your line, and keep product moving into the cold chain.

Why Evisceration Discipline Determines Your Margin

In a 410-beast cycle, every minute of delay between bleeding and evisceration raises bacterial load and lowers cold room efficiency. At scale, a 0.5% contamination rate across 410 carcasses means two full carcasses condemned. At a conservative $2,500 per carcass on the hoof-to-cold-room value chain, that is $5,000 lost per cycle. Run 250 cycles a year and you are looking at over $1.2 million in avoidable loss. The lessons below are written to protect that margin.

Initial Incision and Bleeding Procedures

Bleeding must be complete before evisceration begins. Incomplete bleed-out leaves residual blood in the thoracic and abdominal cavities, which darkens meat, shortens shelf life, and complicates organ inspection. For cattle, the standard is a high neck cut severing both carotid arteries and the jugular vein. For smaller ruminants, a transverse cut across the throat below the jaw achieves the same result. Bleed time should be a minimum of 6 minutes for cattle and 3 minutes for sheep and goats under African ambient conditions, where higher temperatures accelerate coagulation and spoilage.

Stunning must precede bleeding. Penetrative captive bolt is the most common method in commercial African abattoirs, with electrical stunning used for smaller species. Confirm insensibility before the cut: no corneal reflex, no rhythmic breathing, no vocalisation. Record stun-to-bleed interval. Anything over 60 seconds is a welfare and quality failure.

Evisceration Steps for 410 Beasts

Evisceration follows a fixed sequence. Deviate and you will puncture the rumen or intestines, spilling contents across the carcass and forcing a full wash-down that adds 8â12 minutes per carcass. For a 410-beast line, that is 55â80 hours of lost throughput per cycle.

Step 1 â Open the abdomen. With the carcass suspended on the rail, make a midline incision from the brisket to the pelvic bone. Use a brisket saw or knife with a guarded tip. Do not cut deeper than the skin and subcutaneous fat in the first pass.

Step 2 â Open the chest. Split the sternum with a brisket saw or cleaver. Expose the thoracic cavity. This releases the vacuum that holds the pluck (heart, lungs, trachea) in place.

Step 3 â Tie off the oesophagus. Locate the oesophagus at the diaphragm. Double-clamp or tie it with food-grade twine to prevent rumen contents from leaking into the thoracic cavity. This single step prevents the majority of contamination events.

Step 4 â Remove the pluck. Pull the heart, lungs, and trachea free as a single unit. Place on the inspection table immediately. Do not let the pluck rest on the floor or against the carcass.

Step 5 â Remove the stomach complex and intestines. Loosen the attachments of the rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum. Pull the intestinal mass free, keeping the mesentery intact for inspection. Place in the offal chute or trolley.

Step 6 â Remove the liver and gall bladder. Separate the liver from its attachments. Inspect for flukes, abscesses, and discolouration. Remove the gall bladder without puncturing it â bile taints meat and is a common cause of liver condemnation.

Step 7 â Final cavity inspection. Check the abdominal and thoracic cavities for residual viscera, blood clots, and contamination. Wash down with potable water at 10â15Â°C. Do not use recycled water for final rinse.

Carcass Splitting and Trimming

After evisceration, split the carcass down the midline using a band saw or cleaver. For cattle, split from the pelvic bone through the spine to the neck. Keep the blade clean â a contaminated saw spreads bacteria across both sides of the carcass. Trim any visible contamination, bruises, and injection sites. Trimmed material goes into the condemned bin, not the trim bucket. In African export-oriented plants, trimming standards follow importing country requirements, often stricter than local regulation.

Organ Inspection and Disposal

Every organ set must be inspected by a trained meat inspector. The table below summarises the most common findings and required actions in African abattoir settings.

Table 1: Common Organ Inspection Findings and Disposal Actions
Organ Common Finding Action Disposal Route
LiverFascioliasis (liver flukes)Condemn if extensive; trim if localisedRendering / incineration
LungsPneumonia, abscessCondemnRendering
HeartPericarditis, cystCondemnRendering
IntestinesParasites, haemorrhageCondemn affected sectionsRendering / composting
StomachRumenitis, foreign bodiesCondemn if perforatedRendering
KidneysNephritis, cystsCondemnRendering

Source: FAO Manual on Meat Inspection for Developing Countries (1994), Chapter 4; and OIE Terrestrial Animal Health Code (current edition), Section 6.

Hygiene Practices During Evisceration

Hygiene is not a separate task â it is a continuous discipline. The following table sets out the practical standards for a 410-beast line.

Table 2: Hygiene Standards for Evisceration Operations
Control Point Standard Frequency Verification
Knife sanitisation82Â°C water, 2-minute immersionEvery carcassTemperature log
Hand washingSoap + potable waterEvery 30 minutesSupervisor check
Apron and boot washChlorinated water (50 ppm)Every 2 hoursVisual inspection
Carcass rinse waterPotable, 10â15Â°CContinuousMicrobiological test weekly
Floor drainageFree-flowing, no poolingContinuousHourly check
Offal tableSanitised between speciesEach batchSwab test monthly

Source: Codex Alimentarius CAC/RCP 58-2005 Code of Hygienic Practice for Meat, Sections 5â7; adapted for tropical African operating conditions.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Sharps and Zoonotic Exposure

Evisceration involves continuous contact with sharp knives, saws, and cleavers. In African abattoirs, the most common serious injuries are deep lacerations to the non-dominant hand and forearm. Always wear cut-resistant gloves on the non-knife hand and chainmail aprons where available. More critically, evisceration exposes workers to zoonotic pathogens including Brucella, Mycobacterium bovis, and E. coli O157:H7. Anyone with an open cut on the hand must not work the evisceration line. Pregnant workers should be reassigned away from the line due to brucellosis risk. Report any splash to eyes or mouth immediately and rinse with clean water for 15 minutes. Keep a first-aid log and ensure tetanus vaccination is current for all line staff.

Equipment Sanitisation After Evisceration

At the end of each processing shift, every tool that touched a carcass must be sanitised. Knives, steels, saws, hooks, and the evisceration table are all critical. The sequence is: rinse with warm water to remove organic matter, wash with detergent, rinse again, then sanitise with a food-grade disinfectant (chlorine at 100â200 ppm or quaternary ammonium compound). Air-dry on racks â never towel-dry. Store knives in a dry, clean rack, not in sheaths. Sheaths trap moisture and bacteria. For a 410-beast line, budget 45â60 minutes for end-of-shift sanitation. This is not optional downtime; it is the cost of staying in business.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Confirm stun-to-bleed interval under 60 seconds; bleed minimum 6 minutes for cattle.
  • Tie off oesophagus before opening the thoracic cavity â this prevents the majority of contamination.
  • Remove pluck, stomach complex, intestines, liver, and gall bladder in that order.
  • Inspect every organ set; condemn and route to rendering any organ with abscess, parasite, or discolouration.
  • Sanitise knives in 82Â°C water after every carcass; wash hands every 30 minutes.
  • Split carcass on midline with clean saw; trim all visible contamination and bruises.
  • Rinse cavities with potable water at 10â15Â°C; no recycled water for final rinse.
  • End-of-shift: rinse, wash, rinse, sanitise all equipment; air-dry on racks.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Manual on Meat Inspection for Developing Countries (Animal Production and Health Paper 119)
  • Codex Alimentarius â Code of Hygienic Practice for Meat (CAC/RCP 58-2005)
  • WOAH (OIE) â Terrestrial Animal Health Code, Section 6: Meat Inspection
  • ILO â Safety and Health in the Meat Processing Industry
  • African Union â Interafrican Bureau for Animal Resources (AU-IBAR) Resources

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course Cold Room for 410 Beasts. It is a practical reference only and does not replace national meat inspection regulations or veterinary authority oversight. Always operate under the supervision of a registered meat inspector.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time you have to start bleeding a 410 kg beast after stunning?
quiz.explanation: Bleeding should begin within 60 seconds after stunning to ensure proper blood drainage.

quiz.q: Which tool is recommended for making the initial incision for bleeding?
quiz.explanation: A sharp 6-inch curved boning knife allows a precise cut to sever the carotid artery and jugular vein.

quiz.q: How long should bleeding take for a 410 kg beast?
quiz.explanation: Bleeding typically takes 4 to 6 minutes to ensure complete drainage.

quiz.q: What should you do if the beast shows signs of consciousness after bleeding?
quiz.explanation: If the beast blinks or breathes, it is not fully bled and must be bled again.

quiz.q: What is the first cut made during evisceration?
options: A) From the sternum to the pelvic bone
B) From the throat to the ear
quiz.explanation: The initial evisceration cut runs from the sternum down to the pelvic bone.

quiz.q: Why should you keep the knife blade pointed up during the belly cut?
options: B) To avoid cutting the intestines
quiz.explanation: Pointing the blade up prevents accidental puncture of the intestines, which causes contamination.

quiz.q: What should you use to split the sternum of a 410 kg beast?
quiz.explanation: A meat saw is needed to cut through the thick sternum of a large beast.

quiz.q: How many people are recommended for eviscerating a 410 kg beast?
quiz.explanation: A team of three (cutter, holder, inspector) improves speed and safety.

quiz.q: What should you do if you accidentally cut the intestines during evisceration?
quiz.explanation: Washing with 1% vinegar solution helps reduce bacterial contamination.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time recommended for evisceration per beast?
quiz.explanation: Evisceration should take 12 to 15 minutes to minimize bacterial growth.

quiz.q: What tool is used to split the carcass after evisceration?
quiz.explanation: A meat saw with a 30-inch blade is used to split the spine.

quiz.q: What solution is recommended to wipe the carcass to prevent flies?
quiz.explanation: A 2% salt solution helps deter flies and clean the carcass.

quiz.q: What should be the maximum fat thickness left on the carcass after trimming?
quiz.explanation: Trimming fat to 1 cm thickness meets market standards and reduces waste.

quiz.q: How long should it take to split a carcass manually?
quiz.explanation: Manual splitting takes about 8 to 10 minutes per beast.

quiz.q: What should you do with abscesses found on the carcass?
options: A) Cut them out and discard
quiz.explanation: Abscesses must be removed and discarded to ensure meat safety.

quiz.q: Which organ should be smooth, dark red, and free of spots?
quiz.explanation: A healthy liver is smooth and dark red; spots may indicate disease.

quiz.q: What disease requires you to not open the carcass and call a veterinarian immediately?
quiz.explanation: Anthrax is a serious zoonotic disease; suspected cases require immediate veterinary attention.

quiz.q: How should condemned organs be disposed of?
options: A) Sold at a lower price
B) Put in a pit with lime or burned
quiz.explanation: Condemned organs must be buried with lime or incinerated to prevent disease spread.

quiz.q: How many inspectors are recommended for organ inspection of 410 beasts?
quiz.explanation: A team of two inspectors ensures thorough and efficient inspection.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of chlorine solution for sanitizing knives during evisceration?
quiz.explanation: A 200 ppm chlorine solution is effective for sanitizing knives and equipment.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap and water during evisceration?
quiz.explanation: Washing hands for 20 seconds is recommended to remove bacteria.

quiz.q: What should you do if you drop a knife on the floor during evisceration?
options: A) Wipe it on your apron
quiz.explanation: A dropped knife must be sanitized to prevent contamination.

quiz.q: Why should you use separate knives for opening the belly and cutting meat?
quiz.explanation: Using separate knives prevents cross-contamination between the belly contents and meat.

quiz.q: What is the first step in sanitizing equipment after evisceration?
options: B) Rinse off blood and tissue with warm water
quiz.explanation: Rinsing off blood and tissue first removes organic matter before sanitizing.

quiz.q: How long should knives be soaked in sanitizer?
quiz.explanation: Soaking knives for 2 minutes in sanitizer ensures proper disinfection.

quiz.q: What should you use to dry equipment after sanitizing?
quiz.explanation: Air-drying is best to avoid recontamination from cloths.

quiz.q: How long does it take to clean and sanitize equipment after eviscerating 410 beasts?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and sanitizing equipment for 410 beasts takes about 30 minutes.

quiz.q: What should you wear when handling sanitizer?
quiz.explanation: Gloves protect your hands from the harsh chemicals in sanitizer.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a log of cleaning?
options: B) To prevent cross-contamination between batches
quiz.explanation: A cleaning log helps ensure consistent hygiene and prevents cross-contamination.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of sanitizing equipment after evisceration?
quiz.explanation: Sanitizing kills bacteria and prevents cross-contamination between batches.
